shift n drops the first n positional parameters; default 1; shift 0 changes nothing
shift by more than $# fails with a message (a non-interactive shell may exit)
times writes two lines of user and system times in the form NmN.NNs NmN.NNs
times reports real accumulated times: after burning CPU the shell's user time is not zero
trap action condition... sets the action; it runs via eval when the condition arises
cases: signal/trap_int signal/trap_term signal/trap_hup signal/trap_quit signal/trap_usr2 signal/trap_eval signal/trap_two

statement: trap - condition resets to default; a first operand that is an unsigned integer resets all operands
trap '' condition ignores the signal
$? after a trap action is what it was before the action
Conditions may be EXIT, 0, a name without SIG, or a number
trap with no operands writes trap -- 'action' condition for each condition not at default, quoted for reinput
trap -p writes the action of each named condition, and of every condition with no operand (new in 2024)
note: POSIX.1-2024 addition; dash 0.5.13.4 has no -p, so bash --posix is the oracle

statement: An invalid condition gives a warning and a non-zero status, and the shell does not exit
Traps stay in place until changed; an action can itself set or reset traps
$(trap) in a command substitution shows the parent's traps
The EXIT trap runs in the environment of the last command: variables and $? are visible; it runs once
An EXIT trap set in a subshell runs when that subshell ends; the parent's EXIT trap does not run there
A signal ignored on entry to a non-interactive shell cannot be trapped or reset
note: wolf-lang#681

statement: A trap action runs between commands of a list, loop or function, not only at the end of the script
trap -- action condition is accepted
A signal with a default action of terminate ends the shell with that signal when not trapped; the EXIT trap may or may not run
unset name removes the variable and its export attribute; unset -v the same
unset -f removes a function, and not a variable of that name
unset of a readonly variable fails with a non-zero status
Unsetting IFS, PATH and other shell variables works and has the specified effect
sh -c string runs the string; the next operand is $0 and the rest are positional parameters
sh -c with an empty string exits zero
sh -c reads no commands from standard input, which stays available to the commands
sh file args runs the file with $0 the file name and the operands as positional parameters; the file need not be executable
A command file with no slash is looked for in the current directory first
A command file that cannot be found gives status 127
note: dash 0.5.13.4 exits 2; the sh page says 127, so bash --posix is the oracle

statement: sh -s reads commands from standard input and takes operands as positional parameters; no operands and no -c means -s
The shell does not read ahead on standard input: a command it starts reads the bytes after its own line
A script of only blank lines and comments exits zero; the status is otherwise that of the last command
A syntax error in a non-interactive shell gives a status from 1 to 125
A shell given -i, or reading standard input with input and error on a terminal, is interactive; otherwise not
-c and -s combine with option letters in one argument and with -o
Input lines may be of any length
The shell's own exit: the EXIT status is that of the last command when input ends
An interactive shell ignores SIGQUIT and SIGTERM and survives SIGINT
With -m an interactive shell ignores SIGTSTP, SIGTTIN and SIGTTOU
set -o ignoreeof keeps an interactive shell alive at end-of-file
The command history list: commands typed are kept, at least 128 of them, HISTSIZE and HISTFILE honoured
note: HISTFILE across two sessions has no case: one session cannot show a file read at the next start

statement: set -o vi: ESC enters command mode; motion, editing and history keys as the vi-mode sections list (about 60 commands)
In vi insert mode the erase, kill, ^V, ^W and end-of-file characters act as described
MAIL, MAILCHECK, MAILPATH: the shell tells the user before a prompt when a mailbox file changes
An interactive shell accepts an input line longer than the terminal's own line limit (input lines are of unlimited length)
With no editing mode on, the terminal's erase, kill and word-erase characters edit the line before the shell sees it
Lines that arrive together are run one after the other
ENV is ignored when the real and effective user or group IDs differ
note: needs a set-user-ID shell; not built by the corpus (and wolf has no uid surface, wolf-lang#633)

statement: A FIFO or terminal standard input set non-blocking is put back to blocking reads
note: needs a descriptor inherited with O_NONBLOCK; measured by hand (docs/CENSUS.md)

statement: alias name=value defines an alias; alias name writes it as name=value quoted for reinput; alias alone writes all
alias for a name with no definition fails with a message, and other operands are still processed
unalias name removes it; unalias -a removes all; removing a missing alias fails
An alias may name a reserved word position and aliases apply after reserved words that take a command
An alias defined in a function or compound command is not in effect for the rest of that already-parsed command
Alias names may contain ! % , @ and the portable filename characters
command name runs the utility ignoring functions
command -v name writes how the name would be run: a path, the name of a built-in or function, an alias definition, a reserved word
command -V name writes a description in words for each kind
command -p uses a default PATH that finds the standard utilities
command before a special built-in removes its special properties: errors do not exit, assignments do not persist
The status of command is that of the utility; 127 not found, 126 not executable
command is not a declaration utility by itself, but command export keeps assignment context
type name writes how each name would be interpreted, and fails for a name that is not found
type's output names the path of a utility found in PATH
hash name remembers the utility's location; hash alone lists; hash -r forgets; a missing utility fails
A remembered location that stops working is searched for again
cd with no operand goes to HOME; with HOME unset or empty it fails or does nothing as recorded
cd - goes to OLDPWD and writes the new directory
cd sets PWD and OLDPWD, and they are what a later child sees when exported
cd -L (default) keeps symbolic links in PWD and resolves dot-dot against it; cd -P uses the physical path
CDPATH is searched for a relative operand that does not begin with dot or dot-dot, and the result is written when found there
cd to a missing directory, a file, or with too many operands fails with a non-zero status and PWD unchanged
cd -e with -P exits 1 when the new directory's name cannot be determined (new in 2024)
note: POSIX.1-2024 addition; dash 0.5.13.4 has no -e; bash --posix is the oracle

statement: cd canonicalizes: dot components and repeated slashes are removed from PWD
pwd writes the absolute pathname of the current directory; -L from PWD when valid, -P with no symbolic links
pwd with a bad option fails
echo writes its arguments separated by spaces and a newline
echo with XSI escapes (\c \n \t \\ \0nnn) — recorded from dash, which is XSI; bash --posix differs
note: implementation-defined when the first operand is -n or any operand has a backslash; dash is the oracle because scripts under /bin/sh rely on it

statement: true returns zero and false non-zero, ignoring arguments
test with no operands is false; one operand is true if not null
Two operands: ! negates; a unary primary is applied
Three operands: a binary primary is applied first; then ! with two; then ( x )
Four operands: ! with three
String primaries: = != -n -z, and < > by byte order (new in 2024)
Integer primaries: -eq -ne -gt -ge -lt -le, with signs and leading zeros and blanks
An operand that is not an integer makes an integer primary an error: status above 1
File primaries: -e -f -d -r -w -x -s -L -h
File type primaries: -b -c -p -S -g -u -k, and -t for a terminal
-ef -nt -ot compare two files (new in 2024)
-O and -G test ownership by the effective user and group
note: wolf-lang#633 (no uid surface)

statement: -a and -o and parentheses (obsolescent XSI forms scripts still use)
[ needs a closing ] and reports its absence
-r -w -x reflect the permissions that apply to the caller
printf format with %s %d %c and literal text; the format is reused until operands run out
Escape sequences in the format: \\ \a \b \f \n \r \t \v \ddd
%b interprets backslash escapes in its operand, including \c which stops output and \0ddd
Integer conversions %d %i %o %u %x %X with flags, width and precision
String conversions with width and precision; %c takes the first character; %% is a percent sign
A numeric operand starting with a quote is the character's code
A bad numeric operand gives a diagnostic and a non-zero status, and output still happens
Floating conversions %e %f %g %a (required when the system has them: recorded from dash)
printf with no format operand fails; -- ends options
Numbered argument conversions %n$ (new in 2024)
note: POSIX.1-2024 addition; neither dash 0.5.13.4 nor bash 5.3 implements it; recorded, not counted

statement: read assigns fields split by IFS to the variables; the last gets the rest, trimmed of IFS white space
Without -r a backslash escapes the next character and backslash-newline continues the line; with -r backslash is literal
read returns non-zero at end-of-file, having assigned what it read
read reads exactly one line, leaving the rest of the input for the next reader
read with no variable name: REPLY as an extension, or an error (recorded from dash)
note: POSIX requires at least one var operand; behaviour without one is unspecified

statement: read -d delim reads up to the delimiter; -d '' reads up to a NUL (new in 2024)
note: POSIX.1-2024 addition; dash 0.5.13.4 has no -d; bash --posix is the oracle

statement: read into a readonly variable or an invalid name fails
read uses the shell's IFS when none is given for the command, and does not expand what it reads
read from a descriptor other than 0 through redirection, and from a here-document
getopts walks options, setting the variable and OPTIND; returns non-zero at the end with the variable set to ?
note: dash 0.5.13.4 sets OPTARG to the empty string for an option with no argument, and restarts oddly after OPTIND=1; the page says unset, so bash --posix is the oracle for the getopts cases that show OPTARG

statement: Grouped options, an option-argument in the same word, and -- to end options
An unknown option: ? with a diagnostic and OPTARG unset; with a leading colon in optstring, ? with OPTARG the letter and no diagnostic
A missing option-argument: ? with a diagnostic, or : with OPTARG the letter when optstring starts with a colon
getopts parses explicit operands in place of the positional parameters
OPTIND starts at 1; setting OPTIND=1 restarts parsing; a first non-option operand ends it
getopts in a function uses the function's parameters; OPTIND is a shell-wide variable
wait with no operands waits for every child and returns zero
wait pid returns that child's status; several operands: the status of the last
wait for a pid that is not a child of this shell returns 127
wait reports a child ended by a signal with a status above 128
The status of a child that ended before wait is still collected, for any of the known process IDs
wait with a job ID operand (%1, %%)
wait in a subshell cannot wait for the parent's children
kill pid sends SIGTERM; kill -s name and kill -name and kill -number send that signal; the status of a signalled child shows it
kill -l lists signal names; kill -l number names that signal; kill -l with an exit status names the signal that caused it
kill -0 pid tests for the process without sending; a missing process fails
kill is built in: it signals by job ID (%1), and works on the shell's own children without a search of PATH
kill with a bad signal name or no operand fails
kill accepts several pids, a negative pid for a process group, and -- before it
umask writes the mask as octal; umask -S symbolically; umask mode sets it for the shell and its children
umask accepts a symbolic mode
umask with an invalid mode fails
ulimit -f reports or sets the file size limit in 512-byte blocks; unlimited is written as the word
A file-size limit applies to children: a write past it fails
ulimit -H and -S select hard and soft limits; -a reports all; -c -d -n -s -t -v name resources (new in 2024)
Raising a hard limit without privilege, or a bad operand, fails
fc -l lists the history; fc -l first last selects a range; -n omits numbers; -r reverses
fc -s re-executes a command, optionally with old=new substituted
fc first last edits the commands with FCEDIT or -e editor and then runs the result
fc in a non-interactive shell with no history fails without ending the shell
jobs lists each job: [n], current (+) or previous (-), state, command; -l adds process IDs; -p writes only process group IDs
jobs in a non-interactive shell lists background commands and jobs -p writes their process IDs
A job's state is reported as Running, Done, Done(n), Stopped (signal) as the page lists
fg with no operand runs the current job in the foreground; fg %n that job; its command is written first
fg and bg with job control off fail with a message
bg resumes a suspended job in the background and writes [n] command
Left and right arrows move the cursor; a character typed is inserted there
Ctrl-A and Ctrl-E (Home and End) move to the ends of the line
Ctrl-K kills to the end of the line; Ctrl-D deletes the character under the cursor
Up and down arrows walk the history, and a recalled line can be edited
Ctrl-R searches the history backwards as the pattern is typed
Tab completes a file name, and a command name in command position
Alt-B and Alt-F move by words
In a UTF-8 locale backspace erases one character, and the cursor moves by characters, whatever their byte length or width
test -r, -w and -x answer for this process's access (a mode-000 file is unreadable to a user, an executable is executable), -L/-h for a link, -ef for two names of one file
note: from the script census: `test -x` is false for an executable regular file, `-w` true for a read-only one, `-r` true for a mode-000 one, `-L`/`-h` false for a symbolic link, `-ef` false for two links to one file (XCU test). The most-counted gap: git's test-lib, ltmain.sh, debconf's confmodule, every init script, `service`, `which`. Since sh07 the primaries read `fs_stat`/`fs_lstat` and decide access by the shell's own effective ids (`/proc/self/status`, else `id`); a read-only or noexec mount, ACLs and capabilities are where this can still part from access(2) (W07).

statement: umask sets the mask that files made by the shell and its children receive, and reports it in octal and with -S
note: from the script census: `umask` is not implemented ("not supported yet", status 2) (XCU umask). install-sh, mkinstalldirs, config.guess, lesspipe and two Debian postinst scripts stop or misbehave on it.

statement: trap takes a condition as a signal number for every signal it takes by name (1 2 13 15, 14), and lists it by name
note: from the script census: `trap action 13` (a signal number with no wolf meaning) is refused with "no such condition" and status 1 where dash and bash record it (XCU 2.15 trap, XSI numbers). `trap action PIPE` by name is accepted. Seen in config.guess, test-driver, tap-driver.sh, ylwrap, configure. Since sh07 13 and the other numbers every host agrees on (4, 5, 8, 11) are taken and listed; catching SIGPIPE still waits on wolf-lang#679.

statement: A bracket expression holding a slash matches a slash in a case pattern and in the four trim forms (the explicit-slash rule is for file names only)
note: from the script census: `case` and ${x#pat}: a bracket expression that contains `/` matches a slash (XCU 2.14.1; the explicit-slash rule of 2.14.3 is for pathname expansion only). Stops every autoconf configure at its directory check; also ylwrap. Fixed in sh07: the slash rule is applied only to pathname expansion.

statement: A pipeline stage inside a command substitution writes to a descriptor the substitution duplicated (exec 4>&1), not to the shell's own output
note: from the script census: In `$( exec 4>&1; { echo x >&4; } | cmd >&3 )` the stage's write to descriptor 4 does not reach the substitution (it is empty) (XCU 2.7.5, 2.12). zdiff, zgrep and xzgrep read a decompressor's exit status this way and fail.

statement: Unquoted $* on the right of an assignment or as a case word joins with the first character of IFS
note: from the script census: Unquoted `$*` on the right of an assignment (and as a `case` word) joins with nothing instead of the first character of IFS (XCU 2.5.2). configure computes host_os as `linuxgnu`, so every `*-gnu*` host check takes its default arm (two checks answer "guessing no", two extra checks run). Fixed in sh07.

statement: Any byte but NUL is data: bytes above 0x7f pass unchanged to a program's arguments, file names, read, command substitution and here-documents
note: from the script census: Every byte above 0x7f becomes `?` when a word is handed to a program as an argument or a file name, when `read` reads it, and in a here-document (XCU 2.2: only NUL is excluded). update-ca-certificates loses a certificate whose file name is not ASCII. Since sh07 valid UTF-8 passes unchanged everywhere (quote/utf8_bytes); a byte that is not UTF-8 still cannot be a wolf `str` (W06), so the statement stays pending on quote/c_s_high_bytes.

statement: . reads any readable file, not only a regular one: /dev/null is an empty script, a FIFO is read
note: from the script census: `. /dev/null` (and a FIFO, /dev/stdin) is "not found", which ends a non-interactive shell with status 2 (XCU 2.15 dot). pfetch does `. "${PF_SOURCE:-/dev/null}"` and prints nothing. Since sh07 `.` reads /dev/null and a FIFO (builtin/dot_fifo_program); builtin/c_s_dot_special_file has the shell write the FIFO from an in-process background subshell, which waits on fork.
